content:
<Rep. Jamie Raskin>: I oppose H.R. 1071, the ``No Censors on Our Shores Act,'' as ordered reported by the Committee. This bill would create new and extremely vague and confusing inadmissibility and deportability grounds in our immigration laws. Specifically, it would make inadmissible or deportable a ``foreign government official'' who ``was responsible for or directly carried out'' an act against a United States citizen located in the U.S. when that act ``would violate the First Amendment'' ``if committed by a United States government official in the United States.''
At markup, the Republican majority stated that the intended purpose of H.R. 1071 is to punish foreign officials who purportedly censor U.S. citizens' speech from abroad. I assumed our Republican colleagues meant to focus on the clear cases of authoritarian leaders who have jailed and persecuted people for daring to exercise fundamental human rights to speak freely, exercise their religious beliefs, or report on information critical of tyrannical and authoritarian governments around the world--like Vladimir Putin's jailing of American journalists like Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich. I thought we might hear about Chinese pro-democracy activists who have faced harassment, threats and violence from their government directed against Uyghurs, Tibetans and other critics, or perhaps about Saudi Arabia's treatment of human rights activists, including slain Washington Post contributor, Jamal Khashoggi, who was assassinated by agents of the Saudi Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman, simply for writing essays in favor of democratic liberty for his country.
But instead, the Majority has focused its rhetorical fire on our European allies, who share our country's traditional commitment to human rights and the cause of liberal democracy across the globe. This gives me serious pause. Moreover, there are significant questions about how this bill would function in practice. As a preliminary matter, notwithstanding the Majority's assertions, the bill's scope is not limited to the First Amendment's free speech protections but also covers ``any act'' that ``would violate the First Amendment.'' This sweeping scope could lead to some unintended consequences. For example, if the Pope of the Roman Catholic Church--who is also a head of state--demotes a Catholic Bishop in the U.S. for ideological or doctrinal reasons, under this legislation, the Executive Branch would arguably have the authority to deny the Pope as a public official entry into the U.S. for violating the Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses of the First Amendment.
The operative language of the bill is also quite vague, raising troubling questions about the scope of its application. It targets government officials who are ``responsible for or directly carried out, at any time, the commission of any act against a United States citizen located in the United States.'' (Emphasis added). If this bill were enacted, would:
• a German judge be inadmissible if the judge
orders the takedown of Holocaust denial speech visible
to Germans in Germany but posted to X by an American in
the U.S. if X--out of convenience--chooses to remove
the post entirely rather than blocking it only for
German users?
• a British judge be inadmissible if the judge
finds that an article written in the U.S. by a U.S.
citizen but reprinted in the United Kingdom (UK) is
libelous and subject to a takedown order under UK law
because that ruling ``would violate the First
Amendment'' ``if committed by a government official of
the United States?''
• a British judge or official who enforces the
UK's campaign finance laws be inadmissible in a case
where a dual citizen of the U.S. and the UK wants to
contribute money directly to a candidate (which is not
allowed there) or spend money on UK election ads in
amounts that exceed that country's campaign finance
limits, given that there is a recognized right under
Buckley v. Valeo to contribute to candidates and to
spend unlimited money on campaigns and political money
is treated as a form speech under the First Amendment?
In addition to substantive concerns, this bill is unworkable in practice because it empowers Executive Branch officials to make the determination that an act by a foreign official is one that ``would violate the First Amendment'' ``if committed by a government official of the United States.'' These officials would likely be making these decisions without the benefit of an extensive record present in an American court case or any extensive familiarity with First Amendment doctrines and case law, even setting aside the fact that those doctrines and case law are constantly evolving.
Even if the authority granted to Executive Branch officials under H.R. 1071 gives them the discretion to not enforce the Act's provisions in a given case, the availability of such discretionary authority would not solve the problems highlighted by the foregoing examples. Indeed, it might prove more problematic, because Executive Branch officials would have the discretion to pick and choose which U.S. citizens' rights should be vindicated by deporting or denying a foreign official entry into the U.S.
Democrats allowed this bill to pass on voice after the Majority promised to work to address our constitutional concerns and expand the scope of this bill to address more pressing freedom of expression issues in the U.S. and around the world. However, in light of the Administration's increasing efforts to attack Americans' freedom of speech here in the United States and to use taxpayer resources to prop up extremist parties abroad, it became clear that a compromise bill was no longer a viable option.
Since this bill was voted out of Committee, we have seen this Administration--and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) specifically--persistently violate American citizens' constitutional rights, including the First Amendment right to speak freely and protest the government. We have seen DHS agents break into people's homes without warrants, wrongfully detain U.S. citizens, and murder American citizens right here in the United States.
We have also seen the Administration double-down on efforts to intervene in the domestic politics of European countries to boost MAGA-aligned extremist movements. Last November, the White House's National Security Strategy spelled out a policy of ``Promoting European Greatness,'' an unsubtle signal that the MAGA movement now has its sights on promoting right-wing movements in Europe. The strategy called for the U.S. government to promote ``patriotic European parties.'' Committee Republicans last year invited a member of the UK parliament-- whose fringe political party holds only five seats in the House of Commons--to testify before this Committee in an effort to platform and mainstream his extremist views. In February, the State Department announced it would fund efforts to boost extremist parties in Europe, under the guise of protecting ``free speech.'' And just a few weeks ago, President Trump filmed a message from the Oval Office pledging his ``complete and total endorsement'' to the Putin-backed authoritarian Viktor Orban in Hungary's upcoming elections.
While the President and his allies in Congress attempt to impose their extremist MAGA views on our democratic European allies under the guise of defending free speech, the Trump Administration continues its vicious and, in many ways, unprecedented attack on Americans' freedom of speech and protest, freedom of assembly, freedom of the press, academic freedom and intellectual freedom right here at home.
Handing this Administration greater authority and standardless discretion to harass, intimidate and bully people with whom they disagree, in the U.S. and around the world, is not something we can support in the midst of this dramatic crackdown on political freedom in America. As a result, I must oppose this flawed legislation, and I urge all of my colleagues to do the same.
Jamie Raskin,
Ranking Member.
